what: Associated Banc-Corp is a bank in the upper Midwest. It takes deposits and makes loans across Wisconsin, Illinois and Minnesota, lending to businesses, financing commercial property, writing residential mortgages and providing wealth management to individuals.
customers: Small and mid-sized businesses, commercial property owners, homeowners and retail depositors across its three-state footprint, plus wealth management clients.
money: The spread between interest earned on loans and paid on deposits.
Wealth management, service charges, card and mortgage banking fees.
moat: A bank’s real assets are its deposit base and its local lending relationships, both built over decades. Associated has a long-established position in Wisconsin in particular, where it holds a substantial share of deposits — and low-cost deposits from customers who do not move are the only genuine advantage in banking.
risks: Commercial real estate exposure is the sector’s main concern and is a meaningful part of the loan book.
The upper Midwest is a slow-growing region demographically, which limits organic loan growth.
Results depend on interest rates set by the Federal Reserve rather than on anything management decides.
Revenue history is uneven, at $1.1B in 2023 and $1.0B in 2024 before $1.5B in 2025, reflecting balance sheet repositioning.
Ten analysts average a $34.40 target, about 16% above the current price.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 10.2 times earnings, 5.1 times EV/EBITDA and 6.5 times free cash flow.
A net margin of 31.9% is solid for a bank of this size.
A strong, long-established deposit franchise in Wisconsin provides low-cost funding that competitors cannot easily take.
Wealth management fee income diversifies the revenue away from pure interest rate dependence.
watch: Net interest margin and non-performing loans. The margin tells you what the bank earns on its balance sheet; the problem loans tell you what it is about to give back.
view: Banking is a business where the deposit side matters more than the loan side, and this is consistently underweighted by people analysing banks. Anyone can make loans — the competition to lend is fierce and the pricing reflects it. What is hard to acquire is a base of customers who leave their money with you at low rates and do not move. Associated has that in Wisconsin, built over many decades, and it is the asset that makes the bank worth owning.

The footprint is both the strength and the ceiling. Wisconsin, Illinois and Minnesota are stable, diversified economies with established businesses, which produces good credit experience and loyal depositors. They are also slow-growing demographically, which means organic loan growth is limited and a bank in this region grows by taking share or by acquisition rather than by riding regional expansion. That caps what this can be, and it is why the multiple is 10.2 times earnings rather than something higher.

The commercial real estate exposure is the question the whole sector is being judged on, and the honest answer for any regional bank is that it is not yet knowable. Commercial property losses emerge slowly: a loan does not default until it matures and cannot be refinanced at current rates. That means two or three more years of maturities before the picture is clear, and a bank that looks fine today can look different after them. Associated’s position is not obviously worse than peers, which is the most that can be said.

The revenue history — $1.1 billion, then $1.0 billion, then $1.5 billion — reflects balance sheet repositioning rather than underlying volatility, and it makes the trend harder to read than it should be. At 10.2 times earnings with a solid deposit franchise and a conservative region, this is a reasonably priced regional bank rather than a bargain. Net interest margin and non-performing loans are the two numbers, and of those, non-performing loans is the one that turns a fair investment into a bad one.
bull: A low-cost Wisconsin deposit franchise funds steady lending through the cycle, commercial real estate losses stay contained, and 10 times earnings proves conservative.
bear: Commercial real estate losses emerge as loans mature and cannot refinance, while a slow-growing region offers no loan growth to offset them.
